summary: Investment banks and brokers are having a strong year on volumes, but the pace is uneven. Goldman earned an 18.7% return on equity in Q3 and Morgan Stanley's equities revenue rose 41% [1][2], while Schwab, Interactive Brokers and Robinhood posted record client activity or assets [3][4][5]. Dealmaking cooled: global M&A fell 41% from Q2 as the 10-year Treasury yield reached 5.34% [6]. The Fed is holding at 3.75% to 4.00% with two members wanting a hike [7]. The Financials sector trades at 15.0 times forward earnings against 17.7 for the S&P 500 [8]. We see a group priced for solid, not heroic, earnings.

watch: Whether M&A closings rebuild after Q3's 41% fall in announced and completed value, with Goldman's fee backlog lower than at the end of Q2 [1][6].
A 10-year Treasury yield at 5.34% and a Fed with two dissenters favoring a hike could tighten financing for deals and IPOs [6][7].
Retail trading intensity: Schwab's daily trades rose 44% y/y and Interactive Brokers' DARTs rose 18%, so any fade from these levels would show up quickly in commissions [3][4].
The US capital-rule rewrite proposed in March 2026 would cut required capital for the largest banks, but it is still a proposal [9].
Net interest income at brokers depends on rates and client cash: Robinhood's fell 9% while Schwab's rose 14% [5][3].

basics.intro: These companies sit between people or companies that need money or advice and the markets that provide them. Investment banks advise on mergers and help firms sell shares and bonds, then trade securities for clients. Brokers let investors buy and sell and earn from commissions, fees on client assets and interest on cash and margin loans. GICS puts Goldman, Morgan Stanley, Schwab and Robinhood here; large universal banks such as JPMorgan sit in diversified banks, and asset managers sit in a neighbouring sub-industry.

products.name: Advisory (M&A)
products.what: Advice on buying, selling or restructuring companies. Banks earn a fee, usually only when a deal closes.
products.examples: Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, PJT Partners, Evercore

products.name: Underwriting
products.what: Banks buy new shares or bonds from an issuer and resell them to investors, keeping a small spread or fee.
products.examples: IPOs, follow-on share sales, investment-grade and high-yield bonds

products.name: Sales and trading
products.what: Banks make markets for clients in shares, bonds, currencies and commodities, and finance hedge funds through prime brokerage.
products.examples: Goldman Sachs Equities and FICC, Morgan Stanley Equity

products.name: Retail brokerage
products.what: Platforms where individuals trade shares, options and crypto. Revenue comes from interest on cash and loans, order flow and subscriptions.

products.name: Wealth management
products.what: Advisers manage client portfolios for a percentage of assets, a recurring fee that rises with markets.
products.examples: Morgan Stanley Wealth Management, Raymond James Private Client Group, LPL

products.name: Principal investing and lending
products.what: Firms put their own balance sheet into loans, private funds and stakes, earning interest and investment gains that vary from quarter to quarter.
products.examples: Goldman Sachs private banking and lending and Investments

terms.meaning: Fixed income, currencies and commodities: the trading desks that make markets in bonds, currencies and raw materials.
A fee for deal advice, typically a percentage of deal value paid when the deal completes, which is why closings matter more than announcements.
Fees banks expect to earn from deals already signed or mandated but not yet completed. It is a lead indicator for banking revenue.
The difference between the price a bank pays an issuer and the price it sells securities to investors, which is its fee for taking the risk.
Pay as a share of net revenue. Staff are the main cost, so the ratio is the key lever on margins and flexes with revenue.
Money and securities held for customers. Brokers and wealth managers earn fees on these assets, so they are the base for recurring revenue.
Deposits of cash and securities by clients minus withdrawals, excluding market moves. It shows whether a platform is genuinely gaining customers.
Daily average revenue trades: a measure of how often clients trade, and so of commission revenue.
Interest earned on client cash, margin loans and securities less interest paid to depositors. For retail brokers it is often the largest revenue line.
A loan a broker makes against a client's portfolio so they can buy more securities. It earns interest but rises and falls with markets.
Payments some retail brokers receive from market makers for routing client orders to them. It is controversial and regulated.
VaR estimates likely trading losses; CET1 is the core equity capital a bank must hold against its risks. Rules on both limit how much risk dealers take.

drivers.name: Deal activity
drivers.how: Advisory and underwriting fees follow the number and size of completed deals and new issues. They swing sharply with confidence, stock prices and borrowing costs.

drivers.name: Market volatility and volume
drivers.how: Trading revenue and retail commissions rise when markets move and investors act. Very quiet or very panicked markets can both hurt.

drivers.name: Asset levels
drivers.how: Wealth and brokerage fees are a percentage of client assets, so rising stock prices and net inflows lift revenue with little extra cost.

drivers.name: Interest rates
drivers.how: Higher rates raise income on client cash and loans, but also raise financing costs for deals and can slow issuance.

drivers.name: Capital rules
drivers.how: Regulators set how much equity banks must hold against trading and lending. Lower requirements free capital for buybacks or more trading.

drivers.name: Pay and talent
drivers.how: Staff pay is the largest expense, and star bankers and advisers can move clients. Pay flexes with revenue, which cushions profits in bad years.

business: Revenue comes from four streams: advisory and underwriting fees, trading, fees on client assets, and net interest. Goldman's Q3 net revenue of $18.68B included $3.22B of investment banking fees, $3.47B from FICC and $6.44B from equities [1]. Schwab earned $3.48B of net interest revenue and $1.91B of asset management and administration fees in the same quarter [3].

Customers are corporations, governments and funds on the institutional side, and households on the retail side. Morgan Stanley reported $10.5 trillion of client assets in its wealth and investment businesses [2]. Schwab held $13.33 trillion [3]. Raymond James and LPL serve independent advisers and their clients [10][11].

People are the largest cost. Raymond James posted a 19.5% pre-tax margin for fiscal 2026 [10], while Interactive Brokers, a highly automated platform, reported 78% in Q3 [4]. Technology, compliance and interest expense follow. PJT's adjusted pre-tax margin was 18.8% in Q3 [12].

Pricing power depends on franchise strength. Top advisory banks win mandates on relationships and execution, so fees hold; trading and retail commissions are close to commodities. Schwab and Interactive Brokers compete on cost and scale. We think rankings matter: in the first nine months Goldman led global equity underwriting and JPMorgan led debt, per LSEG [13].

Big balance sheets hold securities, client receivables and loans funded by deposits, repo and debt. Goldman reported a standardized CET1 ratio of 12.4% at 30 September [1]. Raymond James reported a 23.2% CET1 ratio [10]. Brokers also carry client money, held as liabilities, which is the base for interest income [3].

The industry is mixed. Advisory boutiques like PJT carry no funded debt and hold $766 million of cash [12], so they are asset-light. Banks and large brokers are balance-sheet heavy: they need capital for trading and lending and must meet regulatory capital rules [1][9].
overview: In the US, FINRA-registered broker-dealers had gross revenues of $776.8B in 2025, up 7.5%, and pre-tax income of $115.0B, up 33.8% [14]. Global investment banking activity is huge: M&A of $3.9 trillion in the first nine months of 2026, up 28% [6]. Damodaran's January 2026 data had 32 firms in this group, a small, listed core [15].

Main segments are advisory and underwriting, sales and trading, retail brokerage, wealth management and principal investing. Equity underwriting reached $870.7B in the first nine months of 2026, with IPOs at $214.4B [13]. The wealth and retail pools are far larger: Schwab alone holds $13.33 trillion of client assets [3].

These firms sit between issuers and investors. Suppliers are technology vendors, exchanges, clearing houses and funding markets; customers are companies, funds and households. Their fees depend on what companies do with capital, and on the level of markets that sets asset-based fees [14][3].

The industry moved from commission-based to asset-based and interest income. Schwab's net interest revenue is $3.48B against $1.16B of trading revenue [3], and Robinhood's transaction-based revenue of $867M is now paired with $415M of net interest [5]. Retail participation grew: 58.0% of households owned stocks per the Fed data SIFMA cites [14].

The US dominates. It holds 43.7% of global equity market value ($68.9 trillion) [14]. Wall Street banks lead global league tables: JPMorgan, BofA Securities, Morgan Stanley, Citi and Goldman were the top five in debt underwriting for the first nine months [13]. Asia Pacific M&A was $242B in Q3, up 36% y/y [6].
competition: Significant competitors number in the dozens globally, but a handful dominate. Damodaran's January 2026 dataset counts 32 listed firms in this industry [15]. The US has 3,184 FINRA-registered broker-dealers, down 2.0% [14]; most are small and offer retail or niche services.

Leaders in banking are the big US houses. LSEG's first nine months ranking had JPMorgan first in debt underwriting followed by BofA Securities, Morgan Stanley, Citi and Goldman, with Goldman first in equity underwriting [13]. In retail, Schwab holds $13.33T of client assets [3] and Interactive Brokers $964.7B of customer equity [4]. Share data for advisory was not publicly available in the sources we opened.

Overall it is concentrated at the top and fragmented below it. A few global banks win the largest mandates, while boutiques such as PJT and Evercore compete on independence. Retail brokerage is concentrated among a few platforms, with Robinhood at 28.7M funded customers [5] and Interactive Brokers at 5.58M accounts [4].

Barriers to entry are high for the full-service bank: capital, a global client base, trading technology and regulatory approval. Basel and surcharge rules set how much capital the largest firms must hold [9]. Barriers are lower in retail apps, which is how Robinhood grew to 28.7M funded customers [5].

Economies of scale matter in trading, technology, clearing and balance sheet. Schwab's 52.7% pre-tax margin and Interactive Brokers' 78% come from low-cost platforms spread over large client bases [3][4]. Scale also lets Goldman and Morgan Stanley finance clients and win large deals [1][2].

The mix is split. Retail execution and plain trading are near-commodities, where cost decides; advisory, underwriting leadership and wealth relationships are differentiated by people and trust. Morgan Stanley's wealth pre-tax margin of 30.4% suggests that advice earns more than trading [2]. This is our reading of that figure.

Customers hold the power in trading and underwriting, where large issuers and funds shop banks against each other. Suppliers matter less, though the funding market and talent do: pay is the main cost [10]. Retail clients can move assets fast, but net inflows suggest platforms are winning: Schwab's core net new assets were $190.4B in Q3 [3].
drivers: Revenue growth follows activity: deal values, issuance, trading volumes and client assets. Q3 global M&A of $993B fell 41% from Q2, yet nine-month equity issuance rose 62% [6][13]. Schwab's net new assets of $190.4B and Morgan Stanley's $232.4B added to recurring fees [3][2].

Operating margins depend on revenue mix and pay. Fee-based wealth and retail platforms hold steadier margins: Schwab's was 52.7% [3]. Advisory boutiques saw PJT's margin slip to 18.8% from 21% when completions fell [12]. Because staff cost is semi-fixed in the short run, revenue swings hit margins.

Key cost variables are staff pay, technology, interest paid on funding and client balances, and legal and compliance. Schwab's non-interest expenses rose 9% y/y while revenue grew 17% [3], showing operating leverage. Raymond James's pre-tax margin was 20.2% in Q4 [10].

Interest rates cut both ways. Higher rates lifted Schwab's net interest revenue 14% and Interactive Brokers' by 19% [3][4], but the 10-year Treasury yield reaching 5.34% weighed on deal values in Q3 [6]. The Fed held at 3.75% to 4.00% on 28 October with two dissents for a hike [7].

Inflation, GDP and commodity prices act mainly through markets and confidence. Reuters tied the Q3 M&A slowdown to higher borrowing costs and surging energy prices [6]. Strong GDP and profits help issuance: S&P 500 Q3 earnings growth was 31.4% [8]. We could not source a direct figure on unemployment sensitivity.

The group is cyclical with a growing recurring base. Deal and trading revenue follow the cycle, while asset-based fees grow with savings and markets. Retirement assets reached $53.6 trillion in 2025 [14]. Pre-tax income for US broker-dealers jumped 33.8% in 2025, showing how large the swing can be [14].
financials: Growth is lumpy. Goldman's Q3 net revenues rose 23% y/y but fell 8% from Q2 [1]; Raymond James's fiscal 2026 net revenues rose 12% to $15.79B [10]. Damodaran's January 2026 data shows analysts expecting 20.3% five-year earnings growth for the group, a high bar [15].

Margins vary by model. Damodaran's industry net margin is 14.45% and gross margin 53.27% (Jan 2026; the page's column labels were garbled, so we matched values by position) [15]. Schwab earned a 52.7% pre-tax margin, Interactive Brokers 78%, Raymond James 19.5% for the year and Morgan Stanley's firm margin was 32% [3][4][10][2].

Returns are strong at the top. Damodaran's ROE for the industry is 17.77% [15]. Goldman's Q3 annualized ROE was 18.7% [1], Schwab's 25% [3], Raymond James's fiscal-year ROE 18.7% [10] and Morgan Stanley's ROTCE 22.6% [2]. ROIC is not meaningful for balance-sheet firms; we did not source one.

Leverage is high, as with all financial intermediaries. Damodaran shows debt to book capital of 79.15% and market debt-to-equity of 135% for this group [15]. Regulators watch capital instead: Goldman's standardized CET1 was 12.4% [1].

Free cash flow is hard to define for firms whose assets are securities, so analysts use earnings and payout. Asset-light boutiques generate cash: PJT held a record $766M of cash with no funded debt [12]. Large banks return capital within the limits of their CET1 ratios [1]. We did not source a free-cash-flow yield for the group.

Capex is modest compared with revenue; technology and offices rather than plants. Compensation and technology are the main operating costs [10][3]. The heavy capital need is regulatory capital, set by rules still being rewritten [9]. We did not find a sourced capex-to-sales ratio for the group.

Valuation: Damodaran's January 2026 data gave a forward P/E of 19.86 and PEG of 0.98 for the group [15]. The iShares U.S. Financial Services ETF, a broader financials basket, traded at 19.90 times earnings and 2.47 times book on 9 November [16]. FactSet puts the whole Financials sector at 15.0 times forward earnings [8].
risks: Regulation can raise or lower the capital needed to trade. The March 2026 proposals would cut CET1 requirements by 4.8% for the largest banks and change the surcharge in 10-basis-point steps, but they are only proposals (the Fed vote was 6-1) [9]. Retail rules, such as order-flow and best-execution standards, also matter; we did not open a source on those.

Technology disruption is both a threat and a cost lever. Reuters quotes bankers saying AI and data-centre building are driving deal activity [6], while PJT cited uncertainty around AI investment as a drag on closings [12]. In our view, low-cost platforms push brokers toward interest and subscription income; Robinhood has 5.2M Gold subscribers [5].

Demographics favor asset-based fees: retirement assets reached $53.6 trillion in 2025, with IRAs at $18.7 trillion [14]. Wealth firms depend on advisers and aging clients; LPL's 32,597 advisers and Raymond James's $1.94 trillion of client assets show how much rides on advisers [11][10]. Transfer of wealth to younger heirs is a risk we could not quantify from our sources.

Consumer behavior has shifted toward self-directed, app-based investing and more frequent trading. Schwab's daily trades rose 44% y/y [3] and Robinhood has 28.7M funded customers [5]. But activity can reverse, and Robinhood's net interest revenue fell 9% y/y even as transaction revenue rose 19% [5]. Interactive Brokers' DARTs were up 18% [4].

New competitors include fintech apps, private-credit funds that lend without banks, and boutiques. PJT noted that asset managers and LPs are moving toward secondaries and other liquidity options [12]. LPL expects to keep 83% of Commonwealth's assets, below its earlier 90% target, which shows how hard it is to hold client relationships after acquisitions [11].

Geopolitics and energy shocks feed straight into deal volumes: Reuters cited rising energy costs, midterm-election caution and higher rate expectations in the Q3 M&A drop [6]. Asia Pacific M&A still rose 36% y/y to $242B, so exposure is uneven [6]. Trading desks also face sanctions and market-access risk, which we did not quantify.

Substitutes include direct listings, private markets and capital raised outside banks. Private equity-backed M&A had its strongest year to date by value since 1980 records began [6], which keeps banks involved but moves some risk and fees. Companies can also raise money privately; the shift is visible as SpaceX's $86.3B IPO led the 2026 recovery [13].

opportunities: Record issuance and a pipeline of announced deals could convert to completed fees: PJT expects a meaningfully better pipeline entering 2027 [12].
Asset-based income is growing: Schwab's client assets rose 15% to $13.33 trillion and Morgan Stanley took in $232.4B of net new wealth assets in Q3 [3][2].
Lighter capital rules would free equity: the Fed staff memo shows a 4.8% fall in CET1 requirements for the largest banks if the proposals are adopted [9].
Retirement and household savings keep growing, with retirement assets of $53.6 trillion [14].
threats: High borrowing costs could keep deal conversion low, as the 10-year Treasury yield hit 5.34% and Q3 M&A fell 41% [6].
A hawkish Fed could pressure valuations and issuance: two of twelve voters wanted a rate increase on 28 October [7].
A market reversal would hit trading, margin balances and asset-based fees together, after a year in which S&P 500 earnings are projected up 33.3% [8].
Competition from low-cost platforms and private markets could erode commissions and fees [5][6].
horizon.assessment: Our read is that the next three to five years offer solid growth with high variance. The recurring base, meaning asset-based fees, net interest and wealth flows, keeps growing and should cushion bad years. The cyclical part, deals and trading, is at or near records, so a normal slowdown would cut growth even without a downturn. The rate path is the key swing factor: lower rates would help deals but cut interest income, while higher rates do the reverse. Capital relief, if adopted, adds a tailwind that is not yet in the numbers. We think the platforms with the largest client bases and the banks with the strongest advisory franchises are best placed, though this is a judgment, not a forecast, and sources we opened give no consensus long-term estimates.

paragraphs: The cycle looks late but not broken. The Fed held its target range at 3.75% to 4.00% on 28 October 2026 by a 10-2 vote, with two members dissenting in favor of a quarter-point increase, and the statement said inflation remains elevated [7]. For banks, that means funding costs stay high and the next move may be up, not down.

Rates are the main channel into this industry. The 10-year Treasury yield reached 5.34%, its highest since 2002, and Reuters tied that, along with energy prices, to a 41% fall in Q3 global M&A to $993B [6]. Brokers benefit from the same rates: Schwab's net interest revenue rose 14% and Interactive Brokers' net interest income rose 19% [3][4].

Earnings backdrop is strong: FactSet's blended S&P 500 Q3 earnings growth is 31.4%, yet the index's forward P/E has fallen to 17.7 as prices fell 3.9% after 30 September [8]. Fiscal and currency effects were not covered by sources we opened, so we do not comment on them.

Structural demand rests on savings, issuance and trading. US retirement assets reached $53.6 trillion in 2025 and household liquid financial assets $80.4 trillion, with 58.0% of households owning stocks [14]. Those pools feed wealth and retail fees: Schwab's client assets reached $13.33 trillion, up 15% [3].

Capital raising is the other leg. Global equity issuance reached $870.7B in the first nine months of 2026, up 62%, and debt issuance topped $10 trillion, a record [13]. Global M&A was $3.9 trillion year to date, up 28%, although deal count fell 8% [6]. SIFMA put 2025 global equity issuance at $573.8B [14], so 2026 is running well above last year.

Demand is highly cyclical: Q3 equity issuance fell 26% and debt 17% from Q2 [13]. Platform growth is steadier. Robinhood's funded customers rose 7% to 28.7M [5] and Interactive Brokers' accounts rose 35% [4]. We think retirement saving and wealth growth are the durable drivers, with deals adding variance.

Using Porter's five forces: rivalry is intense in trading and retail, where cost decides, and more moderate in advisory. The threat of new entrants is low for global banks because of capital rules, but higher for apps; Robinhood now has 28.7M funded customers [5]. Barriers include capital, licenses and relationships [9].

Buyer power is high in underwriting and trading, where large issuers and funds shop banks against each other. Supplier power is mainly talent and funding: Raymond James and LPL spend heavily to recruit and keep advisers [10][11]. Substitutes include private markets, with private-equity-backed M&A the strongest by value since 1980 records began [6].

Concentration is high at the top. JPMorgan led debt underwriting and Goldman equity underwriting in the first nine months of 2026, with Morgan Stanley in the top three of both [13]. Schwab has $13.33 trillion of client assets, and LPL has 32,597 advisers [3][11]. Moats are franchises, scale and trust; pricing power is strongest in advisory and weakest in commissions. The 3,184 registered broker-dealers fell 2.0% in 2025 [14].

Regulation is the biggest policy factor. On 19 March 2026 US agencies proposed a revised Basel III endgame, a new G-SIB surcharge method in 10-basis-point steps and changes to standardized risk weights; a Fed staff memo estimated aggregate CET1 requirements would fall 4.8% for the largest banks. The Fed voted 6-1 with Governor Barr dissenting [9]. These are proposals, not final rules.

Political and macro factors matter for deals: bankers cited US midterm-election caution, diesel prices and rates as brakes on Q3 activity [6]. PJT said the regulatory backdrop for deals is now more favorable but that elevated rates, geopolitics and volatility make closings harder [12].

Technology is both a cost and a threat. Reuters reports that AI and data-centre investment is driving deal activity [6], while PJT noted uncertainty around AI investment [12]. Low-fee platforms have forced the industry to rely on interest and subscriptions: Robinhood had 5.2M Gold subscribers, up 34% [5]. Legal, social and environmental factors were not covered in the sources we opened, so we leave them out.

Industry economics are good in a strong year. US broker-dealers had $776.8B of revenue, $661.8B of expenses and $115.0B of pre-tax income in 2025, a pre-tax margin of about 14.8% by our calculation, with profit up 33.8% [14]. Damodaran's January 2026 data shows an ROE of 17.77% and a net margin of 14.45% for 32 firms [15].

Margins differ by model. Schwab's pre-tax margin was 52.7% and its expenses grew 9% against revenue growth of 17% [3]. Interactive Brokers earned a 78% margin [4]. Raymond James reported 19.5% for the fiscal year [10], and PJT's adjusted margin fell to 18.8% from 21% [12]. Operating leverage is high: fixed staff costs make profits rise faster than revenue in good quarters.

Returns are healthy: Goldman's Q3 ROE was 18.7%, Schwab's 25%, Raymond James's 20.6% for the quarter and Morgan Stanley's ROTCE 22.6% [1][3][10][2]. Capital intensity is high for balance-sheet firms, with Goldman at a 12.4% standardized CET1 ratio [1]. We could not source a free-cash-flow figure for the group.

Reported earnings are strong. Goldman's Q3 EPS was $17.01 on net revenues up 23% y/y, though revenue fell 8% from Q2 [1]. Morgan Stanley earned $3.03 against $2.80 [2], Schwab's adjusted EPS was $1.69, up 29% [3], and Raymond James earned $3.40 for the quarter [10]. Robinhood's diluted EPS fell 16% to $0.51 as net income dropped 14% [5].

Forward signals are mixed. Goldman said its investment banking fee backlog fell from the end of Q2 and slightly from the end of 2025 [1]. PJT expects record full-year advisory revenue and a better pipeline entering 2027, but lower conversion of announced deals [12].

At the sector level, FactSet shows blended Q3 earnings growth of 6.4% for Financials against 31.4% for the S&P 500 [8]. We could not find consensus estimates specific to this sub-industry. Our view differs on one point: with Q3 M&A down 41%, banking revenue in Q4 is more likely to normalize than to repeat the Q2 peak [6]. That is judgment, not a sourced forecast.

FactSet puts the Financials sector at 15.0 times forward 12-month earnings on 5 November, the lowest tier among sectors alongside Energy at 11.7, against 17.7 for the S&P 500, whose 5-year average is 19.8 and 10-year average is 19.1 [8]. This is sector-wide and includes banks and insurers, not just this sub-industry.

For the sub-industry itself, Damodaran's January 2026 data had a forward P/E of 19.86, a current P/E of 26.81, expected five-year growth of 20.3% and a PEG of 0.98 across 32 firms [15]. The iShares U.S. Financial Services ETF, a broader basket, had a P/E of 19.90 and price to book of 2.47 on 9 November [16]. Those figures are older or broader, so treat them as context.

Our read: on these figures, the group is priced for earnings growth near the top of its range, with a PEG around 1 depending on estimates [15]. A 20% growth assumption is demanding for businesses whose banking and trading revenue just hit records. We could not source a normalized-earnings or free-cash-flow yield for the group, so we do not give one.

Price momentum is positive but not extreme. The iShares U.S. Financial Services ETF returned 5.80% year to date to 9 November on NAV, and sat at $97.12 against a 52-week range of $80.12 to $98.70, near the top [16]. The S&P 500 closed at 7,353.73 on 5 November [8] versus 6,845.50 at the end of 2025 [14], about 7.4% higher by our calculation, so the financials basket looks roughly in line to slightly behind, though the two measures differ (NAV total return versus price).

The ETF has $2.28B of net assets at a 0.37% expense ratio [16]. We did not find sourced short-interest, hedge-fund positioning or flow data for the group, so we do not comment on them. Client flows are a better signal: Schwab's core net new assets were $190.4B in Q3 [3], Morgan Stanley's wealth net new assets $232.4B [2], and Robinhood's net deposits $15.7B [5].

Breadth of fundamentals is wide: Goldman, Morgan Stanley, Schwab and Raymond James all reported higher y/y revenue [1][2][3][10]. The weaker spots are advisory boutiques such as PJT, whose Q3 revenue fell 14% [12], and the risk that elevated trading at Schwab and Interactive Brokers fades [3][4]. Market-wide, the S&P 500's forward P/E has compressed from 22.0 to 17.7 this year [8].
